old: The read loop compiled from C reaches 66.8 GB/s, which is 1.5 loads of 16 B per cycle.
This loop is the C function k_read in bench/bandwidth.c.
It adds every 8 B word of the buffer into one of 16 running sums, and gcc 14.2 chooses the instructions.
The asm loop is written by hand and only loads.
The machine code of k_read on CRB was read with objdump -d on 2026-11-11, with no test run [results/probe-20261111T210017Z.txt].
For each 128 B the loop runs 16 instructions: 4 LDP q (8 loads of 16 B), 8 vector adds, 2 integer adds, one compare and one branch.
So the compiled loop does issue one vector add per 16 B load.
The binary that was read is the build of 2026-11-02 from the current source file.
The 66.8 GB/s was measured on 2026-10-30 with an earlier build, and no copy of that binary was kept.
A copy of the source file of 2026-10-30 holds the same k_read, and the same write and copy functions (k_write and k_copy) [~/workspace/titan/exec/scratch-relocated/ed41c79f/bandwidth.c.orig].
The compiler package on CRB was the same on 2026-10-30 and on 2026-11-11 [results/20261030T193108Z/sysinfo.txt; results/probe-20261111T210017Z.txt].
The build of 2026-11-02 lies between these two days.
So the three loops compiled from C were very probably the same.
The limit of two vector adds per cycle can explain at most part of the gap between 66.8 GB/s and the 134.4 GB/s of the load pipelines.
The core has two vector pipelines (FP/ASIMD 0 and 1), and Arm's table gives 2 vector adds per cycle [SOG, Table 2-1 page 13 and Table 3-15 page 26].
Two adds per cycle allow 2 loads per cycle, which is 89.6 GB/s.
The measured 66.8 GB/s is 25 % below that.
Arm's guide also limits how many operations the core dispatches in one cycle [SOG, section 4.1 "Dispatch constraints", page 55].
Dispatch is the step before the pipelines.
A dispatched operation waits for its inputs and then goes to a pipeline [SOG, section 2.1 page 11].
So a dispatch limit can be higher than the number of operations that the pipelines accept in one cycle.
This report calls these limits dispatch limits.
The section lists eight of them.
The dispatch step handles at most 10 instructions per cycle.
The guide counts instructions after decoding and calls them MOPs (macro-operations).
At most 6 operations per cycle are dispatched for the load pipelines.
The guide calls operations µOPs (micro-operations).
It gives no count for LDP q.
This report counts one LDP q as two operations, one for each 16 B load (est.).
At most 2 operations per cycle are dispatched for FP/ASIMD 0, and at most 2 for FP/ASIMD 1.
On average the loop runs 3.0 instructions, 1.5 loads of 16 B and 1.5 vector adds per cycle.
The four other limits are 20 operations per cycle in total, and 4, 4 and 2 operations per cycle for three groups of integer and branch pipelines.
The loop is below these too on average (est.).
One pass of the loop (128 B) has about 20 operations: 8 loads, 8 vector adds, 2 integer adds, one compare and one branch.
One pass takes 5.37 cycles at 32 KiB (see "Observation" below).
That is 3.7 operations per cycle.
At most 4 of the 20 operations are integer or branch operations.
That is at most 0.75 operations per cycle.
So the loop stays below every limit that was checked: 3 loads per cycle, 2 vector adds per cycle, and the eight dispatch limits.
The check compares average rates only.
It covers only these limits.
It does not exclude any other limit, whether the guide lists it or not.
The cause of the remaining gap is not established.
Observation: one pass of the loop (128 B, 8 loads and 8 adds) takes 5.37 cycles at 32 KiB and 5.34 cycles at 1 MiB.
Each load and each add writes one vector register.
So the loop writes 2.98 to 3.00 vector registers per cycle, half of them by loads and half by adds.
Two readings fit this number.
Hypothesis A: loads and adds that write vector registers share a limit of 3 per cycle.
Hypothesis B: the adds reach only 1.5 per cycle for a reason that is not known, and the loads follow the adds.
The loop also runs 3 instructions per cycle.
A general limit of 3 instructions per cycle does not fit.

The write and copy loops compiled from C have 4 and 5 instructions per pass, and they run about 4 and about 5 instructions per cycle at 32 KiB and 1 MiB [results/probe-20261111T210017Z.txt; results/20261030T193108Z/bandwidth.csv].
The test that separates A and B is a loop with loads and adds in a 3:2 ratio.
Hypothesis A predicts 80.6 GB/s for that loop.
Hypothesis B predicts 100.8 GB/s.
A result of 134.4 GB/s, the limit of the load pipelines, would reject both.
Not run.
